micro.title: Sliding window — add one, remove one, keep the rule

sections.title: Micro-theory (10 minutes)
sections.body:
Every window problem is Day 1's running state, plus the ability to **remove** the element that leaves.

✍️ **Fixed window (size k).** Each step: add `a[i]`, remove `a[i−k]`, record once `i ≥ k−1` ([[sw-fixed-window#template]]).
✍️ **Variable window.** Expand `r` every step; while the window breaks the rule, shrink from `l`; record the length after shrinking ([[sw-variable-window#template-longest]]).
✍️ **Budget form.** "At most k bad things inside" → count the bad things; valid ⇔ bad ≤ k ([[sw-variable-window#budget]]).
✍️ **Why it is O(n)** even with a `while` inside the `for`: `l` only moves forward, at most n times in total ([[cx-amortised-analysis#counting-trick]]).
- Windows need a monotone rule — counts of characters are always fine; sums with negatives are not ([[sw-monotonicity-requirement#decide]]).

sections.title: Pattern card
sections.body:
✍️ FIXED — add a[i]; if i ≥ k: remove a[i−k]; if i ≥ k−1: record.
✍️ LONGEST VALID — for r: add; while invalid: remove a[l++]; best = max(best, r−l+1).
✍️ SHORTEST VALID — for r: add; while valid: record; remove a[l++].
✍️ BUDGET — bad ≤ k. Replacement: bad = len − maxCount.

drill.title: Grumpy Bookstore Owner
drill.statement: Customers arrive each minute; on grumpy minutes they leave unsatisfied. The owner can stay calm for one block of m consecutive minutes. Maximise satisfied customers.
drill.approach: Base = customers on non-grumpy minutes. Slide a window of size m summing customers on grumpy minutes inside it (the extra gained); answer = base + max window.
drill.trigger: "choose one block of exactly m consecutive minutes" → fixed window.
drill.details:
**Task.** A shop is open for n minutes. In minute i, `customers[i]` people come in. If `grumpy[i]` is 1 the owner is grumpy that minute and those customers leave unsatisfied; otherwise they are satisfied. Once, the owner can force themselves to stay calm for `minutes` consecutive minutes. Return the maximum number of satisfied customers.

**Input:** integer arrays `customers` and `grumpy` of length n, and an integer `minutes`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ minutes ≤ n ≤ 2·10⁴; 0 ≤ `customers[i]` ≤ 1000; `grumpy[i]` is 0 or 1.

**Example:** `customers = [1,0,1,2,1,1,7,5]`, `grumpy = [0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1]`, minutes = 3 → `16`. Staying calm for the last three minutes adds 1 + 5 to the 10 who were already satisfied.

drill.title: Substrings of Size Three with Distinct Characters
drill.statement: Count the length-3 substrings whose three characters are all different.
drill.approach: For each i ≥ 2 check s[i], s[i−1], s[i−2] are pairwise different (or keep counts in a size-3 window).
drill.trigger: "substrings of length k" with a per-window property.
drill.details:
**Task.** Count the substrings of length exactly 3 in which all three characters are different. The same substring counts each time it occurs.

**Input:** a string `s`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 100; lowercase letters only.

**Example:** `"xyzzaz"` → `1`: of `xyz`, `yzz`, `zza` and `zaz`, only `xyz` qualifies. `"aababcabc"` → `4`.

drill.title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K
drill.statement: Among windows of length k whose elements are all distinct, return the largest sum (0 if none).
drill.pattern_name: Fixed window with a count map and a distinct counter
drill.approach: Slide a window of size k keeping sum and a frequency map; the window qualifies when the number of distinct keys equals k.
drill.trigger: "length k" + "all distinct" → fixed window + frequency map.
drill.details:
**Task.** Look at every contiguous subarray of length exactly k whose elements are all different. Return the largest sum among them, or 0 if no such subarray exists.

**Input:** an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. **Output:** an integer (can exceed 32 bits).

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ k ≤ length ≤ 10⁵; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[1, 5, 4, 2, 9, 9, 9]`, k = 3 → `15`, from `[4, 2, 9]`. The windows containing two 9s do not qualify. `[4, 4, 4]`, k = 3 → `0`.

drill.title: Maximum Erasure Value
drill.statement: Pick one contiguous block with no repeated values; your score is its sum. Maximise the score.
drill.pattern_name: Variable window with no repeats (sum instead of length)
drill.approach: Exactly Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, but record the window sum instead of the length.
drill.details:
**Task.** Erase exactly one contiguous block of the array in which every value is different. You score the sum of the erased values. Return the maximum possible score.

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 10⁵; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁴.

**Example:** `[4, 2, 4, 5, 6]` → `17`, from `[2, 4, 5, 6]`. `[5, 2, 1, 2, 5, 2, 1, 2, 5]` → `8`, from `[5, 2, 1]` or `[1, 2, 5]`.

drill.title: Find the Difference of Two Arrays
drill.statement: Return the distinct values that appear only in the first array, and those that appear only in the second.
drill.approach: Build a set for each array; collect values of set A not in set B, and of set B not in set A.
drill.trigger: "present in one but not the other" → two hash sets.
drill.details:
**Task.** Given two arrays, return two lists. The first holds the distinct values that occur in `nums1` but not in `nums2`; the second holds the distinct values that occur in `nums2` but not in `nums1`. Order within each list does not matter.

**Input:** integer arrays `nums1`, `nums2`. **Output:** a pair of integer lists.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ lengths ≤ 1000; −1000 ≤ values ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 3]`, `[2, 4, 6]` → `[[1, 3], [4, 6]]`. `[1, 2, 3, 3]`, `[1, 1, 2, 2]` → `[[3], []]`.

sections.title: Concept
sections.body:
✍️ **Abstraction** = exposing *what* an object does and hiding *how*. Callers depend on an interface, not on implementation details.
✍️ In C++ an **abstract class** has at least one **pure virtual** function (`virtual void draw() = 0;`). It cannot be instantiated; derived classes must override the pure virtual functions to be concrete.
✍️ An **interface** (C++ convention) is an abstract class with only pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor. Java has a separate `interface` keyword; a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.
✍️ The four pillars of OOP: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism.

sections.title: C++ example
Interview questions
sections.body:
✍️ **Q: Abstract class vs interface?** An abstract class can have data members, constructors and implemented methods along with pure virtual ones; an interface has only pure virtual methods (no state). Use an interface for a capability shared by unrelated classes; an abstract class for a common base with shared code.
✍️ **Q: Abstraction vs encapsulation?** Abstraction is a design idea (hide complexity, show the essential interface); encapsulation is the mechanism (bundle data + methods, restrict access).
✍️ **Q: Can an abstract class have a constructor?** Yes — it runs when a derived object is created, to initialise the base part.
- **Q: What happens if a derived class does not override a pure virtual function?** It is also abstract and cannot be instantiated.
- Real-world framing interviewers like: a payment gateway, a logger, a database driver — code against the interface so implementations can be swapped (the Dependency Inversion principle from SOLID).
